narrative.overview: CozyVTT is a quiet, adaptable frame around a living game. The shared scene, the current decision, and the people at the table carry the visual energy; application chrome is compact, stable, and willing to recede. Warmth comes from proportion, tactility, and authored campaign content rather than literal wood, parchment, medieval ornament, or a page-wide sepia wash. The product is an object-first workbench. On desktop, the map or primary authored object occupies the stage while party context and session tools live in restrained rails. On tablet and mobile, the same regions become task-focused views reached through a persistent, thumb-friendly navigator. Layout is owned by CozyVTT and exposed through named, versioned regions: plugins may contribute to, order, resize, and hide those regions, but never replace the campaign shell with arbitrary unscoped UI. The interface borrows Shuv to Code's spatial clarity, information density, continuous activity flow, and quiet stateful chrome without becoming a developer tool. Cards remain available for genuinely discrete authored objects. Ordinary structure uses alignment, tonal surfaces, lists, dividers, and whitespace. Mechanics and tool output remain prominent only while active, failed, or consequential, then collapse into readable summaries.
keyCharacteristics: A dominant authored stage with compact contextual instruments.
Warm, genre-neutral surfaces that let campaign art and themes provide flavour.
Dense but calm utility chrome designed for long sessions.
Continuous activity streams with progressive disclosure for mechanics.
Responsive workspace regions shared by core features and plugins.
Visible focus, honest state, and no horizontal overflow at supported sizes.

rules.name: The One Signal Rule
rules.body: Action Amber is the only general action accent and occupies less than ten percent of a normal screen; its rarity makes it legible.

rules.name: The Flat Canvas Rule
rules.body: Canvas and structural surfaces are solid colours by default. Page-wide decorative gradients and default glass panels are forbidden.

rules.name: The Campaign Owns Flavour Rule
rules.body: Genre colour belongs to maps, portraits, system modules, themes, and campaign contributions, never to mandatory shell ornament.

rules.name: The Stable Chrome Rule
rules.body: Theme display faces may decorate campaign identity, but navigation, controls, mechanics, and long-form activity always use the body family.

rules.name: The Quiet Hierarchy Rule
rules.body: Size changes are small and deliberate; establish hierarchy with weight, position, rhythm, and colour before increasing type size.

rules.name: The Flat-by-Default Rule
rules.body: If every region casts a shadow, none of them has meaningful elevation. Resting workspace structure is tonal and border-led.

rules.name: The Map Exception Rule
rules.body: Controls placed directly over artwork may use a compact opaque surface and overlay shadow for legibility; transparency must never reduce control contrast.

dos: Do keep the map, shared fiction, or current authored object visually dominant.
Do use 8px controls, 12px authored surfaces, compact 12–16px gaps, and one-pixel boundaries to create calm density.
Do use cards for discrete authored objects when they improve recognition.
Do collapse completed mechanics into readable summaries while keeping active, failed, and consequential state visible.
Do make core features register through the same named, versioned workspace regions offered to plugins.
Do provide real mobile play for map viewing, token movement, chat, rolls, character control, initiative, and approvals with 44px touch targets.
Do let campaigns, themes, game systems, and plugins provide contextual flavour inside controlled regions.
Do maintain WCAG 2.2 AA contrast, visible focus, reduced motion, and logical reading order.
donts: Don't build “a generic dashboard made from repeated equal-weight cards and hero metrics.”
Don't create “a fantasy-themed interface that relies on wood, parchment, medieval type, or other genre assumptions for its identity.”
Don't make “a direct visual copy of Shuv to Code or another developer tool.”
Don't use “page-wide decorative gradients and glass panels as the default structure.”
Don't present “every chat message, dice result, system notice, and tool operation as a separate prominent box.”
Don't allow “plugin interfaces that inject arbitrary unscoped UI, bypass shared components, or determine the campaign shell for everyone.”
Don't squeeze desktop geometry onto a small screen, permit horizontal overflow, or show “a mobile holding screen in place of useful play.”
Don't leave “dense mechanics permanently occupying the interface after their consequence is understood.”
Don't use cards as a reflex for rails, page sections, chat messages, statistics, or ordinary setting groups.
Don't use colour alone to communicate role, selection, health, visibility, initiative, or danger.
